cards.title: Decidability of contractibility for finite two-dimensional complexes
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm that, on every finite nonempty simplicial complex \(K\) of dimension at most two, halts and decides whether \(K\) is simple-homotopy equivalent to a point? Equivalently, can contractibility of all such \(K\) be decided?

cards.why: This is a basic boundary of algorithmic topology: whether a finite two-dimensional description admits any reliable procedure for recognizing a space with no nontrivial homotopy. It separates unrestricted computability from practical simplification and from resource-bounded versions of topological reduction.
cards.status_note: Read the full source introduction, elementary-move definitions and the complete page-four continuation. Checked the full later random simple-homotopy introduction and searched through 12 September 2026. No decision or undecidability theorem for arbitrary finite two-dimensional contractibility was found. Search results on contracting a loop inside a fixed complex, general fundamental-group triviality and Andrews–Curtis examples concern different tasks.

sentences: The input is a finite simplicial complex made of vertices, edges and triangles.
Decide whether expansions and collapses can transform it into a single vertex.
Intermediate complexes may be larger and higher-dimensional than the input.
The algorithm must halt with a correct answer on every input, but no efficiency bound is imposed.
This recognition problem differs from limiting expansions to dimension three or using collapses alone.

cards.definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.

context_blocks.title: The missing question is a recognition problem
context_blocks.text: The source explicitly asks about deciding whether a two-dimensional complex admits a simple-homotopy equivalence to a point. Its separate parameterized problems bound expansions or ask to reach a graph; those are different computational tasks.

context_blocks.title: Balanced presentations capture the algebraic difficulty
context_blocks.text: The source relates this decidability question to recognizing the trivial group from balanced finite presentations, which have the same number of defining relators and generators. Undecidability of the corresponding problem for arbitrary presentations cannot simply be transferred to this restriction. Likewise, a trivial fundamental group alone does not make every two-dimensional complex contractible.

context_blocks.title: The dimension-three move conjecture is separate
context_blocks.text: The stable geometric Andrews–Curtis question asks whether every contractible two-dimensional complex can reach a point using moves of dimension at most three. Here the unknown is whether an algorithm can always decide contractibility, with higher-dimensional intermediate complexes allowed. The source recalls that dimension four already suffices when a contraction exists.

context_blocks.title: Successful simplification experiments are not a decision theorem
context_blocks.text: The 2023/2024 random simple-homotopy paper gives practical simplification methods and successful examples while explicitly retaining the open low-dimensional decidability question. A heuristic that finds reductions on many contractible inputs does not provide a halting, correct procedure for every input.

cards.context:
The source explicitly asks about deciding whether a two-dimensional complex admits a simple-homotopy equivalence to a point. Its separate parameterized problems bound expansions or ask to reach a graph; those are different computational tasks.

The source relates this decidability question to recognizing the trivial group from balanced finite presentations, which have the same number of defining relators and generators. Undecidability of the corresponding problem for arbitrary presentations cannot simply be transferred to this restriction. Likewise, a trivial fundamental group alone does not make every two-dimensional complex contractible.

The stable geometric Andrews–Curtis question asks whether every contractible two-dimensional complex can reach a point using moves of dimension at most three. Here the unknown is whether an algorithm can always decide contractibility, with higher-dimensional intermediate complexes allowed. The source recalls that dimension four already suffices when a contraction exists.

The 2023/2024 random simple-homotopy paper gives practical simplification methods and successful examples while explicitly retaining the open low-dimensional decidability question. A heuristic that finds reductions on many contractible inputs does not provide a halting, correct procedure for every input.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention.
